channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: The IMF's Fiscal Monitor projects global public debt above 100% of global GDP before 2030, and Il Sole 24 Ore reports an IMF forecast of interest payments at 5.3% of GDP in 2031 against 2.8% before the pandemic.
item.description:
China Daily reports that the IMF's latest Fiscal Monitor describes global public debt as historically high and projects that it will pass 100% of global GDP before 2030, and that Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva says rising benchmark yields in advanced economies are raising debt-servicing costs for emerging markets. Il Sole 24 Ore reports that fiscal affairs director Rodrigo Valdés called for lower spending, deficits and debt in the face of rising government bond yields, while overlapping crises have most countries considering higher spending, and that the IMF forecasts interest payments at 5.3% of GDP in 2031 against 2.8% before the pandemic, in an article that says the United States is particularly in the spotlight. Forbes Japan, citing the World Economic Outlook, says net borrowing of developed countries is projected at 5.2% of GDP in 2026, the highest since 2021. The rows do not give the Fiscal Monitor's debt figure for 2026, name the countries behind the 5.3% figure, or give the yield levels behind the warning. All three are media accounts of IMF material.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The Fiscal Monitor figures are projections, and the call for consolidation is a recommendation, not a decision by any government. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, high public debt and rising bond yields raise government borrowing costs and can limit room for infrastructure and subsidy spending, and they feed into private borrowing costs in construction and manufacturing. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, public construction and infrastructure budgets are a source of demand, and tighter budgets or higher financing costs could slow some projects. The rows do not say which countries would cut which spending. Points that may be worth considering include which governments announce consolidation plans, how bond yields develop, and whether infrastructure budgets are affected.

China Daily | Il Sole 24 Ore | Forbes Japan

item.title: US consumer prices rose 3.7% year on year in September against 3.6% expected, with core inflation at 2.6% year on year against 2.5% expected, and CME FedWatch put the chance of a Fed rate rise this month at 37%, up from 22% on Tuesday.
item.description:
MarketScreener reports that US consumer prices rose 3.7% year on year in September and that core prices, excluding food and energy, rose 2.6% against the 2.5% economists polled by Reuters had projected, with higher gasoline prices from the Middle East war a main driver. Commercial Times adds that the market had expected 3.6%, that core CPI rose 0.3% month on month against 0.2% expected, and that, according to the CME FedWatch Tool, the market gives a 37% chance of a Fed rate rise this month, up from 22% on Tuesday. Chinatimes says gasoline prices rose 9.1% in a single month, contributing around half of the overall price increase, the row not saying whether that is the monthly or the annual increase, and that the producer price index for September is expected on 15 October. LiveMint also puts the odds of an October rate rise at 37% and says price pressures broadened beyond energy. The rows do not give the headline monthly rate, the weights behind the gasoline contribution, or the Fed's reaction.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The data show inflation above expectations, with a headline lifted by fuel prices and a slightly higher core figure, and the reports show a higher market-implied chance of a rate rise. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, higher expected policy rates raise financing costs for housing, construction and equipment purchases. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, fuel-driven inflation also enters input and freight costs, while higher rates can weigh on construction and manufacturing demand. The CPI rows do not give the Fed's reaction to this release. Points that may be worth considering include the producer price index expected on 15 October, the Fed's next meeting, and whether core inflation keeps exceeding expectations.

MarketScreener | Commercial Times | Chinatimes | LiveMint

item.title: Singapore's advance GDP estimate shows 5.4% year-on-year growth in the third quarter, down from 6.2%, with construction up 8.8%, manufacturing up 7.5% from 12.9%, and, per Singapore Business Review, lower chemicals and biomedical cluster output.
item.description:
According to the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry, reported by the Straits Times and Singapore Business Review, and as an advance estimate by CNA, Singapore's economy grew 5.4% year on year in the third quarter against 6.2% in the second, and 1.1% on the quarter after seasonal adjustment against 1.5%. Manufacturing grew 7.5% against 12.9%, and Singapore Business Review says growth in the electronics, precision engineering, transport engineering and general manufacturing clusters outweighed output declines in the chemicals and biomedical manufacturing clusters. Construction grew 8.8% against 6.1%, the best of all sectors according to CNA, with Singapore Business Review adding that both public and private construction output were higher, and rose 3.4% on the quarter after a 2.7% contraction. Wholesale growth was driven by machinery, equipment and supplies and by electronics exports. The rows do not give the size of the chemicals decline, say which chemicals segments fell, or break construction down by type of work. The figures are advance estimates.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The release is a national growth figure with sector detail, and the chemicals decline is stated without a size. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, Singapore is a regional hub for chemicals manufacturing and trading, so a fall in its chemicals cluster is one data point on regional chemical output. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, higher construction output supports demand for construction materials in Singapore, while manufacturing growth slowing from 12.9% to 7.5% points to slower expansion among industrial customers. Points that may be worth considering include the final quarterly figures, further data on the chemicals cluster, and whether construction growth continues into the fourth quarter.

The Straits Times | Singapore Business Review | CNA

item.title: GlobalFoundries is to operate two new chip plants in Malta, New York, with up to USD 21 billion in funding from Japan under the US–Japan Strategic Investment Initiative, and one plant is due to open in 2029.
item.description:
AP reports that GlobalFoundries intends to open two factories in Malta, New York, with up to USD 21 billion from Japan, made possible by the Trump administration's trade and investment agreement with Japan: about USD 10 billion would accelerate construction of a factory due to open in 2029 and about USD 10 billion would fund a second plant. The Standard reports that the plants will be jointly owned by Japanese interests and the US government, that GlobalFoundries, majority-owned by Abu Dhabi's Mubadala Investment, will earn fees for operating and building them and for licensing manufacturing technology, and that Apple and Renesas Electronics are among the first customers. The Semiconductor Industry Association says the first investment would add roughly 900,000 300mm wafers of annual US capacity when operational, the second would have similar capabilities, both would be fully funded by Japan, and construction of the first would start later in 2026. The rows do not explain why two tranches of about USD 10 billion are described as up to USD 21 billion, give a date for the second plant or a capacity figure for it, name the chip technologies, or say how many jobs are involved.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The sources describe a funding arrangement and a construction plan, not output, and one plant is due only in 2029. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, chip fabrication uses specialty chemicals and materials supplied to the plant, and government-funded fabs under trade agreements move production capacity between regions. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, electronics adhesives and encapsulants are used mainly in chip packaging and assembly, so any effect on the business would be indirect and several years away. Points that may be worth considering include construction milestones, which suppliers are qualified for the sites, and whether similar Japanese-funded projects follow.

AP | The Standard | Semiconductor Industry Association

item.title: Russian strikes cut power to at least 600,000 people in Ukraine after Trump announced an energy ceasefire on 11 October; Peskov reports no progress, and Zelenskyy says Ukraine has not hit Russian refineries or energy industry in the two days since.
item.description:
POLITICO writes that the energy ceasefire Trump announced on Sunday ended before it had really started: Russian strikes hit 26 energy facilities and four oil and gas sites overnight and in the morning, leaving some 600,000 people without power, while Ukraine has not struck Russian energy sites since the announcement. The South China Morning Post puts the number without power at least 600,000 after ballistic missiles and drones targeted energy facilities in Kyiv, with ballistic missiles also hitting power plants in the Kharkiv region, according to Prime Minister Koretsky. The Economic Times reports Zelenskyy as saying it was the third straight night of Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy sites. Chinatimes reports Russia's Defence Ministry as saying on 14 October that it hit seven energy facilities and a data centre in a large night attack. China Economic Net reports that Kremlin spokesman Peskov said on 13 October there was no new progress on the energy ceasefire announcement compared with 12 October and that the US–Russia diesel agreement is not directly related to Russia's position on Ukraine. It also reports Zelenskyy saying that in the two days since the announcement Ukraine had not struck Russian refineries or its energy industry. BBC reports that UK Prime Minister Burnham, after meeting Zelenskyy, said Ukraine is willing to discuss the ceasefire and that Russia's response was further attacks. The facility counts differ by source, and the rows do not say whether they describe the same attack.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The reports show that the announced truce has not stopped the strikes, and POLITICO describes Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy sites as one of its most effective strategies, which Ukraine has not used since the announcement. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, strikes on power plants and on oil and gas sites reduce Ukrainian industrial output and fuel supply, and a return of Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil facilities would affect Russian fuel and crude exports. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the main channel is energy and fuel costs in Europe, since gas, power and diesel prices feed into production and freight costs. Points that may be worth considering include whether the Kremlin confirms or rejects the truce, whether Ukraine resumes strikes on Russian energy sites, and how oil, diesel and European gas prices respond.

POLITICO | South China Morning Post | The Economic Times | Chinatimes | China Economic Net | BBC News

item.title: The VDMA and ZVEI presidents warn Chancellor Merz not to make export opportunities of parts of industry a bargaining chip in a reported deal with Macron on softer car emission rules and EU-origin subsidy conditions.
item.description:
Neue Zürcher Zeitung reports that the presidents of VDMA, the mechanical engineering association, and ZVEI, the electrical industry association, have written to Chancellor Merz warning that the federal government must not make the export opportunities of significant parts of industry, especially industrial SMEs, a bargaining chip. The letter is directed against an agreement that President Macron and Merz reportedly reached a few days ago. Under it, Brussels' emission-value rules for cars are to be relaxed further to support the struggling European car industry, and Germany is to drop its resistance to a French wish that only vehicles largely produced in the EU's 27 states benefit from state subsidies such as the German premium for electric cars. The row does not give the text of the agreement or the letter, name the export markets or products the associations are concerned about, say how the EU-origin condition would be defined, or report a response from the government. The agreement is described as reported, not confirmed, and the account rests on one outlet.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The letter is a position from two industry associations on an agreement that has reportedly been reached, so it is not a measure. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, content requirements on subsidies shape where vehicles and parts are sourced, and export-oriented manufacturers can be exposed if trading partners respond to such requirements. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the car, machinery and electrical industries are manufacturing customers, so both the relaxation of emission rules and the EU-origin conditions could affect volumes and the sourcing of the materials they buy. The source does not say how large any such effect would be. Points that may be worth considering include whether the German and French governments publish the agreement, how EU origin is defined, and whether trading partners signal a response.

Neue Zürcher Zeitung

item.title: The German government will ask the EU for safeguard measures on Chinese imports in more industries, including chemicals, and EU leaders are due to tell Brussels to come up with new trade tools urgently, reports say.
item.description:
According to informed sources cited by Bloomberg, as relayed by Lianhe Zaobao, the German government will ask the EU to introduce trade safeguard measures that restrict imports of Chinese goods in more industries, including chemicals and mechanical engineering and possibly pharmaceuticals, and the Commission is to be urged to put forward specific plans by the end of 2026. Zaobao gives the EU's trade deficit with China in September as a record USD 34.8 billion. MarketScreener writes that the summit talks in Brussels on Thursday and Friday could address protective measures against chemical imports from China, and notes that the EU and China have agreed in principle to limit imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles. The South China Morning Post reports that EU leaders will instruct Brussels to come up with new "weapons" "urgently" against imbalances they attribute to China's economic policies, and that officials and diplomats in Brussels made clear the hybrid deal is not enough and the EU intends to keep up pressure on China to moderate its exports in other sectors. Handelsblatt lists new protection instruments for the European economy, especially towards China, alongside the EU budget on the summit agenda. The reporting does not say which chemical products would be covered, what form a safeguard would take, whether other member states support the German request, or whether the summit conclusions will mention chemicals. It rests on anonymous sources and on previews written before the summit.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The reports describe an intention ahead of a summit, not a decision, so the reports do not describe any new measure on chemical imports as decided. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a safeguard limits the volume or raises the price of imports from a named origin, and one covering chemicals could change both the cost of materials that European buyers source from China and the competition European producers face from Chinese chemical products. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the effect would depend on whether the covered products are raw materials and intermediates the business buys or finished products it competes with, and the sources do not say which. Points that may be worth considering include whether the summit conclusions name chemicals, which products the Commission's plans would cover by the end of 2026, and whether the approach used for hybrid vehicles is extended to other sectors.

Lianhe Zaobao | MarketScreener | South China Morning Post | Handelsblatt

item.title: VDMA chief economist Johannes Gernandt says about 100,000 jobs in Germany's machinery and equipment industry have been lost since 2019, and that more than 30% of companies will be forced to cut jobs in the coming months.
item.description:
VDMA chief economist Johannes Gernandt says around 100,000 jobs in the German machinery and equipment industry have been lost since 2019. For the coming months, he says 52% of companies expect a stable core workforce, more than 30% will be forced to cut jobs, and fewer than one in five, 18%, plan to hire additional staff. The three shares are given separately and add to slightly more than 100%. The row does not say which companies the percentages cover, when the figures were collected, how many people the industry employs, which segments lost the jobs, or what output, orders or exports lie behind the cuts. It is the industry association's own statement and a single source.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Job losses and expected cuts measure employment at machinery makers, not their orders or output, and the row gives neither. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, machinery and equipment makers are customers for industrial adhesive technologies used in assembly, and a shrinking workforce often accompanies lower or restructured production. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, demand from this group would depend on production volumes and on how much of the job loss reflects efficiency rather than lower output, which the source does not say. Points that may be worth considering include VDMA's next production and order figures, whether job cuts concentrate in particular machine types, and whether the association links them to costs, demand or competition.

VDMA

item.title: The average US 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose to 7.4% on 8 October from 6.66% at the end of August, the highest in nearly three years, and, according to Redfin, September pending home sales fell 4% from August to their lowest since 2014.
item.description:
Bjd.com.cn reports that the average interest rate on a 30-year fixed US mortgage rose to 7.4% on 8 October from 6.66% at the end of August, the highest level in nearly three years. It cites Redfin data released on 12 October showing that pending home sales fell 4% month on month in September, the lowest point since 2014. It also reports, without naming a source, a contract cancellation rate of 14.5%, a record high since 2020. A separate MarketScreener report on San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly says longer-term borrowing costs are higher than the Fed's policy rate and cites mortgage rates "like 7.5%" as an increasingly obvious damper on demand in some parts of the economy. The Daly row does not date the 7.5% or say whether it is the same average 30-year series as the 7.4%. The Bjd.com.cn row does not name the source of the mortgage-rate series, give the number of pending sales, say how many contracts the cancellation rate covers, or give a comparison with a year earlier. It rests on one outlet relaying US data.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The figures show fewer pending sales and a higher cancellation rate, so they describe weaker housing demand rather than building activity. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a higher mortgage rate raises the monthly cost of buying a home, and fewer sales and higher financing costs tend to slow home construction and renovation, which are major end uses for adhesive technologies. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, US construction and do-it-yourself demand could soften if rates stay near this level, while the sources give no figures for housing starts or building-materials sales. Points that may be worth considering include the Federal Reserve's next rate decision, whether pending sales stay at this level in October, and whether home builders report lower orders.

Bjd.com.cn | MarketScreener

item.title: The IEA warns that the global fuel shortage will extend into 2027 despite plans to release emergency stocks or ease trade sanctions, and says record diesel prices are raising the cost of goods and affecting real incomes, economic activity and inflation.
item.description:
The Guardian reports that the International Energy Agency warns the global fuel shortage will last into 2027 despite plans to release emergency stockpiles or ease trade sanctions, and that record diesel prices are already raising the cost of goods and affecting real incomes, economic activity and inflation. Dünya Gazetesi reports IEA President Fatih Birol as saying that the pressure of the US/Israeli–Iran war on energy markets is increasing and has reached fertiliser and other sectors, with LPG prices up 60% on average globally compared with before the war and diesel prices doubled. Birol says the risk could grow with higher winter demand and refineries entering maintenance periods. The reporting does not say which IEA publication or statement the Guardian relies on, what supply and demand figures lie behind the 2027 horizon, which benchmark or region the diesel and LPG comparisons refer to, or what date "before the war" marks. Both are short summaries, and the 60% and doubling figures come from Dünya Gazetesi's account of Birol alone.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The warning gives a longer horizon for the fuel shortage than the stock releases and sanctions easing named in the Guardian's report. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, diesel is the fuel of road freight and much industrial equipment, so a doubled diesel price tends to enter product costs through transport, and LPG is used as a fuel and as a feedstock in parts of the petrochemical chain. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, raw materials, packaging and finished goods move largely by road and sea, so higher fuel prices could reach input and delivery costs with a lag, and customers in construction and manufacturing face the same cost increases. The sources do not say how long prices will stay at these levels. Points that may be worth considering include whether diesel prices ease if the planned stock releases go ahead, how winter demand and refinery maintenance affect supply, and whether freight surcharges follow.

The Guardian | Dünya Gazetesi
